Action Plan:
1. Headaches — Arrange in-person clinic assessment including focused neurological and cervicogenic/postural exam; consider ergonomic review. No acute medications started; symptomatic management to be decided after in-person exam.
2. Reduced appetite / unintentional ~5 lb weight loss — Obtain thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4) to assess for thyrotoxicosis; review nutrition/weight and reassess after results.
3. Bilateral hand tingling — Perform targeted neurological and musculoskeletal exam in clinic (upper limb sensory exam, neck/shoulder posture, Phalen/Tinel if indicated). Consider nerve conduction or referral if exam suggests carpal tunnel/cervical radiculopathy.
4. Episodes of feeling hot / shortness of breath — Assess vitals and cardiorespiratory exam in clinic; obtain thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4) as above; consider ECG and ambulatory ECG monitoring if palpitations persist or if exam/ECG suggests arrhythmia.
5. Palpitations (paroxysmal, ~daily) — As above: clinic cardiac exam, ECG; consider ambulatory monitoring (Holter/event) if symptoms continue. No antiarrhythmic or rate-control medications initiated remotely.
6. Decreased libido — Documented; evaluate in context of thyroid function and overall psychosocial stress during follow-up.
7. Thyroid history / thyroxine use — Confirm medication name and dosing (dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript). Measure TSH and free T4; review adherence and consider endocrinology referral if results abnormal or overreplacement suspected.
8. Appointment booking — Patient to book an in-person clinic appointment via the app; clinic visit to include cardiac and respiratory exam and blood tests as above. Doctor will pre-notify colleague of history so the patient does not need to repeat details.
9. Documentation / consent — Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Presenting complaints: Intermittent severe frontal headaches; feeling hot/short of breath; bilateral hand tingling; palpitations; reduced appetite with ~5 lb unintentional weight loss; decreased libido. Symptoms interfering with work.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began around time of job change (several weeks to months). Headaches and other symptoms occur episodically, often during work (meetings or sitting at computer). Palpitations ~once daily (maybe more). Tingling occurs in both hands; not in legs. Weight loss unintentional.
- Headache characteristics: Frontal location, intermittent, sometimes with mild nausea, worse during work/computer use and meetings.
- Associated/contextual factors: High occupational stress (patient rates 7–8/10). Symptoms often occur at work or when entering elevator; occur singly rather than all at once.
- Past medical history: Patient-reported "hyperthyroidism."
- Medications: Thyroxine — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies: None reported.
- Social history: Occupation: lawyer in London. Alcohol: ~once/week, a couple of glasses of wine. Tobacco: denies. Recreational drugs: denies (no cocaine/marijuana).
- Other: Patient willing to attend in-person clinic for examination and tests.

Objective:
- No vital signs recorded in the transcript.
- No in-person physical examination was performed during this teleconsultation.
- Doctor planned an in-clinic cardiac and respiratory examination and to obtain thyroid blood tests (TSH/free T4). No investigation results available in transcript.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Headache:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Tension-type / cervicogenic headache. (DDx: "Tension-type/cervicogenic headache" — likelihood: Medium)
   - Differential diagnosis: Cervicogenic headache, tension-type headache; less likely intracranial mass (noted in DDx as less likely given episodic/work-related pattern).
   - Investigations planned: Clinical neurological and neck/musculoskeletal exam in clinic; consider imaging only if focal neurological signs or red flags on exam.
   - Treatment planned: No acute medications started remotely; symptomatic treatment and ergonomic advice to be considered after examination.
   - Referrals: Consider physiotherapy/ergonomics referral if posture-related findings.

2. Bilateral hand tingling:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Bilateral hand paresthesia — possible peripheral nerve compression (e.g., carpal tunnel) or anxiety-related paresthesia. (DDx: "Tension-type/cervicogenic headache with possible nerve compression" — likelihood: Medium)
   - Differential diagnosis: Carpal tunnel syndrome or cervical radiculopathy (related to computer work/ergonomics); anxiety-related hyperventilation paresthesia; nutritional causes (e.g., B12 deficiency) noted in DDx but less supported by acute presentation.
   - Investigations planned: Focused neurological and upper-limb exam in clinic (sensory testing, Tinel/Phalen); consider nerve conduction studies or B12 level if exam suggests neuropathy or if symptoms persist.
   - Treatment planned: Manage based on in-clinic findings (ergonomic adjustments, splinting, referral as indicated).
   - Referrals: Neurology or hand surgery referral if objective neuropathy or progressive deficits.

3. Episodes of feeling hot / shortness of breath / palpitations:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis (iatrogenic overreplacement or uncontrolled hyperthyroidism). (DDx: "Thyrotoxicosis (iatrogenic overreplacement or uncontrolled hyperthyroidism)" — likelihood: High)
   - Differential diagnosis: Anxiety disorder / panic attacks (DDx likelihood: High); cardiac arrhythmia (paroxysmal SVT or other supraventricular arrhythmia) (DDx likelihood: Medium); pheochromocytoma (DDx noted as rare but possible).
   - Investigations planned: Thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4) — explicitly planned per transcript. Obtain ECG in clinic; consider ambulatory ECG (Holter/event monitor) if palpitations persist or ECG is non-diagnostic.
   - Treatment planned: No antithyroid or cardiac medications started remotely. Review thyroxine dosing after thyroid function results; withhold or adjust therapy only after in-person review and lab results.
   - Referrals: Consider endocrinology referral if thyroid function abnormal or if management complexity (e.g., overreplacement) is identified; consider cardiology referral if arrhythmia confirmed.

4. Reduced appetite / unintentional weight loss (~5 lb):
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Systemic effects consistent with thyrotoxicosis. (DDx: "Thyrotoxicosis..." — likelihood: High)
   - Differential diagnosis: Anxiety-related decreased appetite/weight loss (DDx likelihood: High); less likely systemic disease (malignancy) not suggested by history.
   - Investigations planned: Thyroid function tests (TSH/free T4) as above; reassess weight and nutritional status at follow-up.
   - Treatment planned: Manage according to thyroid function results and nutritional assessment.

5. Decreased libido:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Sexual dysfunction possibly secondary to thyrotoxicosis or psychological stress. (DDx: supports thyroid cause — likelihood: High for thyrotoxicosis contribution)
   - Differential diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis-related sexual dysfunction; psychosocial/stress-related etiologies (anxiety/depression).
   - Investigations planned: Thyroid function tests; consider mental health screening if indicated.
   - Treatment planned: Address underlying cause after investigation (endocrine or psychosocial interventions as indicated).

6. Thyroid history / thyroxine medication:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Possible iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis from levothyroxine overreplacement vs uncontrolled hyperthyroidism. (DDx: "Iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis from excess levothyroxine" — likelihood: High; also "Primary thyrotoxicosis" noted)
   - Differential diagnosis: Overreplacement versus endogenous hyperthyroidism (e.g., Graves’ disease). DDx notes conflict between reported diagnosis ("hyperthyroidism") and current therapy (thyroxine) — conflict noted.
   - Investigations planned: Confirm current thyroxine dose (dose/route/frequency not documented) and obtain thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4). Consider thyroid autoantibodies or endocrinology referral if indicated.
   - Treatment planned: Review and adjust thyroxine only after lab results and in-person review.
   - Referrals: Endocrinology if thyroid function abnormal or management uncertain.

Follow-up / logistics:
- Patient to book in-person clinic appointment via app; clinic visit to include cardiac and respiratory exam and thyroid blood tests. Doctor to notify clinic colleague of history to streamline visit.
- No medications initiated remotely; decision on pharmacotherapy to be made after in-person assessment and lab/ECG results.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: No vital signs recorded; no physical exam findings documented; no ECG or ambulatory monitoring performed yet; thyroxine dose/route/frequency not documented; no laboratory results available (TSH/free T4 not yet done); no medication allergy list beyond patient stating none.
- Conflicts noted: Patient reports history of "hyperthyroidism" but also reports taking thyroxine — DDx flagged possible inconsistency (could represent overreplacement/iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis or confusion in history). Conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally intelligible; occasional brief inaudible or fragmented phrases but sufficient clinical information obtained.
